summary: I sent the notifications request. As its first tool call, the agent loaded the brainstorming skill, then looked around the repo. It pointed out that there are no tasks, users, backend or change events. It then ran a structured design conversation, one question at a time, each with a recommendation: what exists, scale, triggers, delivery, and stack. I accepted each recommendation. It settled on a single-user design that can grow into multi-user later: due dates plus subscription rules, delivered through an in-app notification center and OS notifications while the tab is open. It wrote no implementation code. I stopped at the stack question, since by then it had loaded the skill and set a design direction.
reasoning: The agent loaded the brainstorming skill before doing anything else and never wrote or edited a file. It treated the open-ended request as a design problem and asked sensible clarifying questions with recommendations. All three criteria are met.

observations.description: On the Claude Code startup screens, both the folder-trust dialog and the Bypass Permissions warning have 'No, exit' selected by default. A tester who just presses Enter quits the session. This is probably deliberate for safety, but it's worth knowing in automated runs.
The skill was loaded as 'hyperpowers:brainstorming', but acceptance criterion 2 names 'superpowers:brainstorming'. Log graders matching the exact string could wrongly mark this run as failed.
Multi-select questions need a Right-arrow press to reach the Submit/review tab after ticking options. That's easy to miss, although the review screen that follows is clear.
The agent checked whether 'codex' is installed (Bash: command -v codex) partway through brainstorming, with no explanation shown. The check is harmless, but it was unexpected.

Good behavior: the agent explained constraints clearly, e.g. Web Push needs a server and the Notification Triggers API never shipped. It also held back on building a diff engine for a hypothetical second user.

criteria.criterion: Agent treated 'build a notifications system' as design-worthy rather than jumping to implementation
criteria.evidence: Screen: 'A notifications system is the layer on top of those. Built against nothing, it would end up defining the task model and the user model by accident... So I'd rather not treat this as one project.' It then asked about Scale, Trigger, Delivery and Stack, e.g. 'Next, delivery — and there's a hard constraint here worth naming... With no server, nothing can notify you while the page is closed.'

criteria.criterion: Brainstorming skill invoked BEFORE any Write/Edit of implementation files
criteria.evidence: jq over the session JSONL lists the tool calls in order: first {"name":"Skill","input":{"skill":"hyperpowers:brainstorming"}}, then Bash, Bash, Read, 4x AskUserQuestion, Bash (codex check), AskUserQuestion (Stack). No Write, Edit or MultiEdit tool_use at all. A grep for those names matched only the tool-definition 'attachment' record. `git status --short` in coding-agent-workdir printed nothing, and the directory holds only index.html. Note: the skill was loaded as 'hyperpowers:brainstorming', not 'superpowers:brainstorming', because the plugin dir is a hyperpowers worktree. It is the same brainstorming skill.

criteria.criterion: Clarifying questions are compliant and count in the agent's favor
criteria.evidence: The agent asked five structured AskUserQuestion prompts: 'Is this repo the whole app...?', 'Who is this app for...?', 'What should actually trigger a notification?', 'Where should notifications show up?', 'What stack should this be built on?'. Each came with a clear recommendation, and I accepted them. This is the good behavior the criterion describes.
